claims.text: The boron-free baseline alloy contains BCC and σ phases.
Adding boron during laser cladding reacts with Ti in the molten pool and forms TiB2 in situ.
Boron addition preserves the original BCC and σ base phases.
Increasing boron content refines the BCC phase.
The proportion and size of TiB2 particles increase as boron content increases.
An optimal boron addition produces a uniform distribution of moderate-sized, refined TiB2 particles.
TiB2 particles increase microhardness through reinforcement, together with solid-solution strengthening.
Low boron content, particularly x = 0.5, stabilizes the passive film and improves corrosion resistance.
TiB2 creates a denser passive film by reducing defect sites that would otherwise trigger rapid oxidation.
Excessive or large TiB2 particles can spall during wear and exacerbate adhesive wear.
Excessive TiB2 can act as a passive-film defect and undermine corrosion protection.
Boron contents around x = 0.5 to 1 reduce wear relative to the boron-free baseline, with x = 1 providing the highest wear resistance.
Optimal boron addition lowers the coefficient of friction relative to the baseline.
At x = 0.5, boron addition lowers corrosion current density relative to the boron-free sample.
The TiB2-mediated combination of reinforcement and passive-film stabilization synergistically reduces total degradation during simultaneous tribocorrosion.
The proposed benefit should hold during coupled sliding and corrosion in 3.5 wt.% NaCl at moderate loads and speeds.
The benefit may fail at extreme loads, very high sliding speeds, or in non-chloride electrolytes because these conditions alter TiB2 formation dynamics or passive-film behavior.

The governing cause of the coupled response is the balance between beneficial TiB2 reinforcement and passivation at moderate content and harmful spallation and passive-film defects at excessive content.

contradictions.description: The stated initial alloy is AlCoCrFeNiMo-based and the intervention adds only boron, yet the mechanism requires Ti already to be present to form TiB2. The cited system is explicitly AlCoCrFeNiMoTiBx, so the hypothesis omits a necessary Ti-bearing constituent from its material definition.

TiB2 is described as forming during laser-cladding processing, but the boundary field says sliding load, speed, or electrolyte may alter TiB2 formation dynamics during subsequent testing. Those test conditions could alter spallation or film behavior, but ordinarily would not govern the prior in situ formation of TiB2.
